subtopic: OIL PRICES-OUTCOME OF DISCUSSIONS WITH PREMIER LOUGHEED
OIL PRICES-OUTCOME OF DISCUSSIONS WITH PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have a question for the Prime Minister. The Canadian Press reported this morning that the Prime Minister said, after his marathon discussion yesterday, that the method of taxation on higher prices was the lone unsettled issue in the current energy negotiations with Premier Lougheed, but the same report quoted Premier Lougheed as saying that progress had been made but a new energy policy was not yet in hand. Therefore, could the Prime Minister tell us exactly what was accomplished at these discussions yesterday, and thus remove the uncertainty and doubt on the part of the public regarding this key issue of national policy? In particular, can he tell us, if

November 28, 1979

there was an agreement on a new oil price, exactly what it will be?

subtopic: OIL PRICES-OUTCOME OF DISCUSSIONS WITH PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, during the meetings between representatives of the Government of Canada and the government of Alberta yesterday, there was agreement on all important principles regarding a pricing policy and the energy package. There was agreement on all major details, with the exception of the detail relating to the mechanism of a tax. It would be my intention to announce the full range of the proposal at the time there is also agreement on the details of the tax.

subtopic: OIL PRICES-OUTCOME OF DISCUSSIONS WITH PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister was not able to tell us when the agreement would come on the details of this tax so I want to ask him, how can there be a budget without first settling this taxation question, which is more than a detail? The Prime Minister said that it could involve more than $5 billion in additional revenue. Surely the Prime Minister is not saying that there can be a valid budget without first having a dear and public answer to this $5 billion question?

subtopic: OIL PRICES-OUTCOME OF DISCUSSIONS WITH PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the budget will set forth quite clearly the assumptions which we believe to be reliable as to the revenue that will come from the tax. All that is at issue is the mechanism of the tax, not its proceeds.

subtopic: OIL PRICES-OUTCOME OF DISCUSSIONS WITH PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Prime Minister why he is not using his authority and assuming his responsibilities to settle this matter now. How long does the country have to wait while he dithers?

subtopic: OIL PRICES-OUTCOME OF DISCUSSIONS WITH PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: OIL PRICES-OUTCOME OF DISCUSSIONS WITH PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: After all, there were disturbing reports last night and today about possible shortages of heating oil in some parts of Canada this winter.

subtopic: OIL PRICES-OUTCOME OF DISCUSSIONS WITH PREMIER LOUGHEED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, barely weeks ago other spokesmen of the Liberal party in this House were urging us not to move as quickly as we are. Now, in that fine Liberal tradition of inconsistency, the hon. member for Windsor West is saying that we are moving too fast.

subtopic: PLAN TO HEAD OFF POSSIBLE OIL SHORTAGE THIS WINTER
PLAN TO HEAD OFF POSSIBLE OIL SHORTAGE THIS WINTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In view of the report last evening to the effect that the National Energy Board has prepared new forecasts regarding the supply and demand of oil this winter, and that in the view of the board the situation and the shortage which was anticipated by the minister and his officials just a month ago, and described by the minister as being "fragile", in fact is worse now, will the minister assure the House that his officials are preparing a plan which will head off this shortage? Will the minister undertake to put this plan before us immediately?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PLAN TO HEAD OFF POSSIBLE OIL SHORTAGE THIS WINTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question and the opportunity it allows me. I saw the report on CTV last night which referred to a secret report of the National Energy Board. I inquired of the NEB with respect to this report and they said that it is simply non-existent, there is no secret report.
The last report put out by the NEB was at the beginning of this month. It indicated that we had a tight, but manageable, situation. They are now getting together the material for the report with respect to the month of November. That report and press release will be put out in the usual manner by the NEB at the end of this month.

subtopic: PLAN TO HEAD OFF POSSIBLE OIL SHORTAGE THIS WINTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as I understand it, the minister is saying that no plan is available. Considering the awful and almost unthinkable situation of a shortage of home heating fuel this winter, is the minister telling us that no effort is being prepared by his government to make available a more equal situation where supply will meet the demand for oil this winter in eastern Canada? Is he preparing a plan that will do this before we wake up some morning to find that people have frozen to death the night before?

subtopic: PLAN TO HEAD OFF POSSIBLE OIL SHORTAGE THIS WINTER
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: PLAN TO HEAD OFF POSSIBLE OIL SHORTAGE THIS WINTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to assure the hon. member that aside from his rather weak attempt at scare tactics, I take the matter very seriously. Indeed we are taking steps with respect to the emergency allocation supply board. We are now consulting with respect to the appointment of that board which in fact will be in place for us in the event that there is an emergency situation and in the event we have to rely on allocation.
I want to assure the hon. member that this government does take its responsibilities seriously in that regard. We are still confident we can get through, and we do not want to cause any undue alarm in respect of the situation. We are, in fact, taking steps to meet that situation and taking a number of initiatives that I have outlined to the House on previous occasions to assure supply over the course of this winter.

November 28, 1979
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN FOOD PRICES-WAR AGAINST INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. Two sets of very disturbing figures have been announced within the past 24 hours. We learned this morning that food prices have gone up by more than 13 per cent, year over year, and yesterday we learned that average weekly earnings are increasing at only 8.6 per cent, well below increases in the cost of living.
While considering that the Prime Minister said inflation was public enemy number one, and considering that the government has already indicated that the forthcoming budget will be a "tough times" budget, will the Prime Minister indicate today one specific weapon he plans to use in fighting the war against his declared public enemy number one?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN FOOD PRICES-WAR AGAINST INFLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the actions taken in the budget and the actions taken by the government generally to bring down the deficit in Canada will certainly be one major instrument in moving the country toward a situation where we can begin to get inflation under control. I know the hon. member shares my understanding that it is not a simple or a new problem, but we are dealing directly with the impact upon inflation of extensive government deficits.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN FOOD PRICES-WAR AGAINST INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister knows that that approach has not worked elsewhere, particularly in the kind of economic circumstances we have now. Even if it had some effect-which 1 do not concede-it would take many, many months to have any bearing on the effects of escalating prices for the ordinary Canadian.
I would like to ask him, in this context, considering that in the province of Ontario, in which this city is located, because of the gap between wage increases and escalating prices the ordinary worker is now losing more than $300 a year in real income, and considering that in the press today the treasurer of the province of Ontario is reported to be urging the Government of Canada to reject the advice of the governor of the Bank of Canada, stating that interest rates should be brought down immediately by 2 per cent, will he at least consider this advice from Canada's largest province, even though he has rejected it from us?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN FOOD PRICES-WAR AGAINST INFLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not read the news reports to which the hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party refers. 1 have not received any communication from the government of Ontario, nor has the Minister of Finance. In any event, it would not be our intention to take the action recommended, at least, by the Leader of the New Democratic Party.

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN FOOD PRICES-WAR AGAINST INFLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister again today has made it clear he intends, as a government, not to act on any single measure to bring down the escalating cost of living in the near future. I would like to ask whether he will announce at least one measure that would have a direct beneficial effect for ordinary Canadians, or will he explain the

insensitivity and apparent hypocrisy of a party that favoured subsidies on certain food items before the election, in order to bring down the price of those items, but since the election has marched off completely in the opposite direction and done nothing to bring down the cost of living for the ordinary Canadian?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN FOOD PRICES-WAR AGAINST INFLATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the New Democratic Party will recognize and, I would hope, admit that there are no shortcuts to the economic problems the country now faces. It is the considered judgment of this government that, facing the extent of economic problems that we do now face, our primary obligation is to recognize that our problems are deeply ingrained and to bring forward in the budget, and in other measures that will come before this House of Commons, measures that are designed to deal with those basic problems. And that is what we intend to continue to do.

subsubtopic: IRAN CRISIS-INQUIRY AS TO MEASURES GOVERNMENT CONTEMPLATES TO HASTEN SETTLEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Could he tell the House what reassuring alternatives his government may have left to progress toward a solution in the matter of the American embassy in Iran?

subsubtopic: IRAN CRISIS-INQUIRY AS TO MEASURES GOVERNMENT CONTEMPLATES TO HASTEN SETTLEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I understand the hon. member's question concerns other actions, other alternatives now available to the government regarding the serious and deplorable situation in Iran. As the Secretary of State for External Affairs and myself have stated many times, we have taken the lead among French-speaking countries and among Commonwealth countries with a view to ensuring the most effective influence on the authorities in Iran. Of course, if there is anything else we can do that would be effective, we will do so.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO REPATRIATE CANADIANS IN IRAN
INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO REPATRIATE CANADIANS IN IRAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I introduced a moment ago a motion under Standing Order 43, which was rejected. It urged the government to play an intermediary role in this crisis.
In view of the far-reaching events the crisis seems to be leading to, I should like to ask whether the government of Canada now sees the necessity of repatriating Canadians now living in Iran?
November 28, 1979

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT INTENDS TO REPATRIATE CANADIANS IN IRAN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we will keep on monitoring this situation, but for the time being we consider the Canadians in Iran can play a valuable role for Canada and for the world.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. Yesterday, the government House leader indicated that the government was prepared to give careful consideration to the statements made by Mr. William Hopper before a House of Commons committee. Mr. Hopper, in that committee, indicated that the continued delay by the government in making a decision on Petro-Canada is causing a high turnover of staff, the passing up of major profitable projects and is generally working against the best interests of the owners of Petro-Canada, who are the people of Canada.
With that statement, can the Prime Minister indicate when the government intends to bring forward its specific proposals on Petro-Canada so that it will not work against the continued best interests of the Canadian people?

Mr. Speaker, without accepting all the implications of that question, 1 am very pleased to receive the assurance of the hon. member- with all the influence that he has with his colleagues-that his party would be prepared to give as speedy as possible passage to measures that we might introduce to put Petro-Canada on a new and more effective footing. We expect to give the hon. member the opportunity to give that bill speedy passage. We hope to have either an announcement or a bill before the House before Christmas.
Once again, I want to express my appreciation and, I am sure, that of the employees of Petro-Canada to the hon. member for his assurance that we will receive speedy passage for those measures.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, 1 would remind the Prime Minister that, unlike the Conservatives, we do not give commitments blindly before we see the exact proposals.
Hear, hear!

We are asking the Prime Minister, when does the government intend to quit dithering and delaying in the development of a proper energy policy? When does it intend to issue its proposals on Petro-Canada? And, just as seriously, when does it intend to make appointments to the energy supplies allocation board so that the board can begin responding to the really dire and emerging shortages of energy
Oral Questions
that are appearing in this country? When will the government begin taking some action, and quit simply talking?

Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member that we recognized upon taking office that one of the great opportunities open to this country and ignored-or, at least, not taken full advantage of-by the former government was the opportunity to build upon the energy strength of this energy-rich nation in an energy-poor world.
It is for that reason that we have given such high priority to bringing together the first ministers of the provinces to meet with me, not simply to discuss the narrow question of price or the narrow question of petroleum but to begin to lay the basis of a genuine national energy program for Canada that can realize energy self-sufficiency by 1990. We are making considerable progress in that direction, and I look forward to being able to keep the House advised of developments. I also look forward to continued support from the House of Commons for that initiative to build on the strength of the country.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT KNOWS DATE OF ANNOUNCEMENT OF ROUTE OF ALASKA OIL
INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT KNOWS DATE OF ANNOUNCEMENT OF ROUTE OF ALASKA OIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the right hon. Prime Minister. According to today's news reports, President Carter has set tomorrow as the ultimate date on which he expects to announce to the American Congress his decision as to the route for the transportation of Alaska oil. On the other hand, the Prime Minister indicated last Friday during his press conference that he intended to phone President Carter to inform him of the route which Canada favours. Could the Prime Minister tell the House whether he has indeed contacted President Carter? Was he aware of President Carter having changed the date for his announcement to the American Congress and, if so, when was he made aware of it?

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER GOVERNMENT KNOWS DATE OF ANNOUNCEMENT OF ROUTE OF ALASKA OIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there has been no change in the time schedule of the American government. I was aware of this rumour, but I am advised that it is unfounded. There has been no change. We are preparing a discussion with President Carter concerning the pipelines.

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL DISCUSS NORTHERN PIPELINE WITH PRESIDENT CARTER
INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL DISCUSS NORTHERN PIPELINE WITH PRESIDENT CARTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a supplementary. Can the Prime Minister tell the House clearly and unequivocally that he indeed intends to make Canada's recommendations in this regard known to the President of the United

November 28, 1979
Oral Questions
States as quickly as possible? Will he assuredly and quickly phone President Carter? I think the issue is quite clear and Canada's preference is well known or at least should be. Is the Prime Minister ready to accept his responsibilities and assure the House that he indeed intends to phone President Carter without further delay, so that the United States is fully aware of Canada's views and that our interest is served?

subtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER PRIME MINISTER WILL DISCUSS NORTHERN PIPELINE WITH PRESIDENT CARTER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Canada has repeatedly expressed its position to the United States. subsubtopic: RISING COST OF LIVING-HARDSHIP CAUSED TO LOWER INCOME CANADIANS
speechtext:
My question is also for the Prime Minister, Mr. Speaker. The figures released by Agriculture Canada today show that the current food price index is 13.1 per cent higher than a year ago, with energy costs, processing, transportation and distribution contributing significantly to that increase. If the government allows energy shortages to develop this winter, and if the oil price also escalates, this situation will get much worse and Canadians on low and moderate incomes particularly will suffer.
The Prime Minister has said that he is considering public policy measures to assist lower income Canadians. The Minister of Finance has said that they must suffer. Will the Prime Minister tell the House which is the policy of this government, and will he move urgently to relieve this anxiety on the part of lower income Canadians?

subsubtopic: RISING COST OF LIVING-HARDSHIP CAUSED TO LOWER INCOME CANADIANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if there is, in fact, a danger of energy shortages this winter it is because the previous government did not act sufficiently to provide guaranteed supplies for Canadians.

subsubtopic: RISING COST OF LIVING-HARDSHIP CAUSED TO LOWER INCOME CANADIANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: RISING COST OF LIVING-HARDSHIP CAUSED TO LOWER INCOME CANADIANS
speechtext: We continue to believe that those kinds of shortages will not occur this winter. But we certainly believe it would have been preferable three years ago for the government which the hon. member then supported to take action which they did not take. In relation to the measures we intend to help people who might be affected adversely or particularly seriously by energy price increases, those will be made clear in the budget.

subsubtopic: REASON FOR LARGE SPREAD BETWEEN WHOLESALE AND RETAIL PRICE OF TURKEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is on the same topic and is addressed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I hope he is in a festive mood this afternoon, because the Minister of Agriculture has released a report which says there is a growing price spread between the retail price and the wholesale price for many commodities. He gave the example of turkey in Toronto, where the spread is some 37 cents per pound.
Has the minister investigated why there is such a large spread between the wholesale and the retail price of turkey? If he has, can he report his findings to the House and tell us what he will do to make sure we have reasonable turkey prices before Christmas?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan Lawrence (Solicitor General and Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Solicitor General of Canada
subsubtopic: REASON FOR LARGE SPREAD BETWEEN WHOLESALE AND RETAIL PRICE OF TURKEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the festive season upon us, I am anxious not to lay an egg. Seriously, with the abolition of price controls and price monitoring by the previous administration, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has no mechanism with which to monitor or investigate that type of occurrence.
I suggest that the mandate of the department at the moment is to investigate price fixing and matters in relation to that. In relation to monitoring ordinary prices and the inflationary trend that is present in the western world today, I think that type of question would be better directed to the Minister of Finance.

subsubtopic: STEPS TO INCREASE CANADIAN PRODUCTION OF VEGETABLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. I hope he will give us a better answer. In his press release this morning, the minister said that the largest increase came from fresh vegetables, an increase of about 5.5 per cent, and many of these vegetables we can produce in this country.
What measures is the minister going to propose to the House to increase Canadian production of vegetables, and can he tell us whether he plans to reinstate the grants program for storing vegetables that was cancelled by the Liberal government a few months ago?

subsubtopic: STEPS TO INCREASE CANADIAN PRODUCTION OF VEGETABLES

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the hon. member's question, I may say that the time the previous government made the decision to close the U.S. border it did, in its wisdom, appoint a monitoring committee made up of a cross-section of the total industry, with representation from the primary sector. Before calling orders of the day 1 wish to advise the House on a matter of procedure.
Shortly after the appointment of Dr. Koester as the new Clerk of this House he set about to initiate a number of practices which might facilitate the operation of the business of the House. This has nothing to do with changes in procedures, discussions of possible changes in procedure, the white paper, for example, tabled by the government last Friday, or any of the work of the standing committee at all. It is not founded on any changes in procedure of any sort.
There is one of such initiatives, however, of Dr. Koester's which is now ready to be put in operation, and that is a private members' business office. It brings together the Deputy Speaker, one of the Table officers and an existing facility, which, within the existing regulations, will process the private members' business. It is strictly in order to facilitate further the conduct of private members' business that Dr. Koester is in the process of establishing the private members' business office. The function of the office will be to assist the Chair on procedural matters relating to private members' business and,
in addition, to advise and assist the members themselves in the conduct of that business.
1 might add that this decision is the result of several discussions which I have had with Dr. Koester and other officers of the House throughout the course of the fall, and it is intended to assist the House with respect to whatever arrangement the House might wish to follow regarding private members' business.
Members, therefore, should be able to avail themselves of this office in the future. It will become a clearing house, as it were, for private members' business, and it will also become a repository of what we hope will be a consistently collected body of opinion respecting procedural decisions from the Chair concerning private members' business.
As I said, it does not in any way change the rights of members to deal with private members' business and the rights of the House in any way. It is simply there to facilitate a collection of the existing jurisprudence on private members' business and to have a group involving the Chair, the Table, and members who are consistently involved in the conduct of private members' business. We hope that it will continue, under Dr. Koester's initiative, to serve the House better in the conduct of its business.

The House resumed from Tuesday, November 27, consideration of the motion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) that Bill C-20, to amend the Income Tax Act to provide a tax credit in respect of mortgage interest and home owner property tax, be read the second time and referred to Committee of the Whole.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TAX CREDIT IN RESPECT OF MORTGAGE INTEREST AND PROPERTY TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) introduced Bill C-20 on November 19 last, he told us he was doing that to give financial help to home owners and people who wish to become home owners. He said, and I quote from page 1461 of Hansard:
This is not an income redistribution measure, this is not an income measure, this is a measure to do with home ownership; with owning a home and with assisting the people of Canada in becoming home owners . . .
Mr. Speaker, the minister is misleading himself stupidly or trying to mislead the House stupidly because in fact one has to be stupid to suggest that, considering the present economic situation, this bill will convince Canadians to buy houses. I think that the Minister of Finance is indeed an intelligent man, that he is not stupid. Therefore, I am led to conclude that he is

November 28, 1979

in fact bound by another election promise by his leader and that unfortunately he can only show off and waste public moneys under the cover of a noble purpose. Obviously it is a noble purpose to help people become home owners, but the Minister of Finance knows quite well that he is making an error by introducing this bill which in fact will encourage nobody to buy a house in such an economic situation. Indeed, editor James G. Ripley of Canadian Building described that situation quite well in his article for the October issue, and 1 quote:

The mortgage interest deductibility scheme, which raised such high expectations during the election campaign, has become as explosive as other hastily improvised "promises" of that time such as the embassy move to Jerusalem and the privatization of Petro-Canada. The reasons are the same: MID was a badly conceived idea, proposed for the wrong reasons, and introduced at the worst possible time.
MID has been condemned by virtually every serious study. Benefits are limited and temporary, but the costs are massive and perpetual. It is a cumbersome, discriminatory, and counterproductive allocation of capital resources. It will distort the tax structure, rental sector, and money markets. And it will increase house costs, interest rates, property taxes, inflation, individual debt and federal deficits.
The reason for this massive subsidy is unadulterated political patronage-the purchase of a few votes in the last election, and a stubborn insistence on paying the "debt" with public funds.
There is an hon. member on the other side who asked: "why did you not promise the same thing?" My answer is that we were more responsible and that we were not there to buy votes.

Mr. Speaker, that irresponsible and shady promise of the Progressive Conservative leader is condemned by experts in both the private sector and the Canadian government. Indeed, in a recent study made by the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation on the deduction of mortgage interest, the conclusions of those government experts are quite harsh for the Clark proposal, and I quote:

A program of mortgage interest deductibility will clearly have a number of implications affecting different sectors of the economy. Most of these appear to be undesirable, as noted.
The last sentence of this study, which has not yet been released by this so-called open government, reads as follows at page 23 of the report:
Mortgage Tax Credit
The recommendation emanating from the discussion of this paper is that a scheme of mortgage interest deductibility should not be introduced in Canada.

Such is the recommendation made by government experts. This, Mr. Speaker, would no doubt explain the rather surprising silence of the minister responsible for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The bill is being considered in the House since November 19 last. Today is November 28. However, the minister who is responsible for housing in Canada has not yet spoken on this bill, the bill which is supposed to be the most important measure of the new government to solve housing problems in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I therefore wonder why the minister responsible for housing remains silent. Why has he not yet spoken about this bill? When will he do so? I know the answer. The minister does not want to speak because he does not believe in this bill. All the experts, the public servants and his provincial colleagues responsible for housing, have told him the same thing-this bill is wrong.
Unfortunately he is also shackled by the nonsensical promises of his leader. He must also support a government which has the audacity to introduce such unfair, useless and costly legislation. 1 have now noted that he has not spoken in this debate. Perhaps he will come to the House tomorrow or the day after to tell us reluctantly that he supports this bill and believes that it is a good bill, but this will be play-acting, Mr. Speaker. It will be simply a theatrical gesture such as the Minister of Finance is so good at doing.
The minister responsible for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation will not delude us if he takes part in this debate because he inadvertently revealed his thoughts in committee to my colleague, the hon. member for Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart), who asked him this question during consideration of the estimates of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation:
Mr. Minister, I would like to know whether you really intend to develop a true housing policy for Canada. When I speak about a true policy, I mean a policy which would consider not only home owners but also tenants, who account for nearly four million Canadians, because if we look at the mortgage tax credit and rebate policy, we can see that it is a policy strictly to the advantage of home owners and to the detriment of tenants.
Mr. Speaker, the minister replied quite candidly:

Well, that is true, sir. It certainly favours and discriminates towards those who own or want to own homes . . . when are we going to have a real housing policy in Canada? 1 think we have had a housing policy in this country that served us reasonably well to this point. As I said earlier, I think we can improve it.

November 28, 1979
Mortgage Tax Credit
In saying that he wanted to improve it, the minister does not say that he wants this piece of legislation to be passed. Here is what he said:
I think there are things that we can do to improve it.
He was talking about a national housing policy in Canada. He continued:
One of the things that you mentioned is important, and that is, what can we do to assist renters, which are particularly numerous in the province of Quebec, as you know.
That is the minister responsible for housing who should be supporting this piece of legislation, but has not yet found time to speak on this legislation. He continued:
I think one of the logical things there that we can work toward is some sort of shelter allowance. I am attracted by this concept. I think it can be used in the field of public housing as well in order to supplement the traditional approach that has existed up to this point.

Well, there it is. The minister told us what he really thinks and, I say so very openly, I congratulate him. He was honest enough to recognize the faults of this bill introduced by the Minister of Finance. He was shrewd enough to identify a logical and fair way of complementing this legislation, making it better, making it fairer and more useful.
1 now ask, will he have the courage to introduce amendments to this legislation to make it a truly efficient tool capable of solving the real housing problems in Canada? I look forward to that. I hope he will have the courage, and particularly the political clout, to convince his colleague, the Minister of Finance, that his bill is bad. For our part, Mr. Speaker, we are determined to fight this legislation. If the government wants to change its mind, if it wants to amend this legislation, if it wants to set up a comprehensive housing policy in Canada, here again we will be pleased and eager to support it. But in the meantime we are going to continue to say this is an unfair, a useless and particularly costly piece of legislation. This piece of legislation, Mr. Speaker, is unfair in that it is biased in favour of the privileged classes in society. Let us remember that the Tory leader made that darned promise on the eve of byelections in Toronto, Winnipeg, Vancouver and Montreal urban and suburban ridings to get a few votes from suburban owners.
The tragedy, Mr. Speaker, is that this has been made into a national policy applicable to all Canadians, both urban and rural, owners and tenants alike, but suitable for only a small number, the richest, the most privileged in our society. That is unacceptable, Mr. Speaker, and I find it is absolutely typical of the Progressive Conservative Party, the party of the multinationals, the party of the oil companies, the party of the more privileged in our society. But I say it is an unfair piece of legislation because it does not meet the needs of too great a number of Canadians. This legislation is unfair to all tenants in my riding of Montreal-Papineau, unfair as well to all other tenants in Canada. It is unfair to all retired people who no longer have a mortgage, who have been able to pay back their

mortgages and who particularly today, at the end of their lives, do not intend to get into debt to benefit from this selective measure of a heartless but politically ambitious Conservative government.
This measure is also superfluous. With the rocketing interest rates it is even less necessary. When we were hit with a three to four per cent leap in interest rates, that meant that one million home owners were left out of the real estate market. They were not attracted to the real estate market as the Progressive Conservative Party, the present government, had hoped. They were excluded from the market because interest rates are much too high. In fact, we must remember this: about four months ago, a family anxious to buy a house with a mortgage of $60,000 needed a yearly income of about $24,000 to realize its dream. Today, to buy the same house, it needs an income of close to $32,000. Such is the result of the economic policy of Progressive Conservatives who allowed an indecent increase in interest rates in Canada. I say this measure is not necessary in the present economic conditions, but with one hand the Progressive Conservative government would like to give some home owners a few hundred dollars, to be exact at most $375 this year, but with the other hand would take away from the same owners $500 to $600 through the higher energy costs that they are arranging behind the scenes with Premier Lougheed of Alberta. So, for all these reasons, this measure is useless, failing as it does to meet the real needs in the housing field. It contains nothing for those who pay too much rent, for those who live in substandard dwellings. We know, for instance, that in urban sectors about 150,000 families are living in unduly small or inadequate dwellings. They cannot afford better shelter unless they spend more than 30 per cent of their income for that purpose. Only 73,000 of all families are living in dwellings that might be improved. Others would have to move to find a decent home. Canada also has about 383,000 decent and spacious units costing more than 30 per cent of income, but obviously that is too expensive. This proposal does not answer the problem.
In presenting this legislation, the Minister of Finance said that in 1982, the last phase of the program, it would cost $2.87 billion. It is much more than expected by the Progressive Conservative Party when it made that electoral promise. It is a shameful waste of public funds, particularly within a context of budgetary restrictions. It is absolutely unjustifiable when spending must be viewed from a thrifty angle. When answering the Minister of Finance, my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), made a proposal that would alleviate the housing problems of Canadians, help three times as many Canadians as would the proposal of the Minister of Finance and be half as costly as the Progressive Conservative program.
Briefly, here are the five major points in my colleague's proposal: a housing allowance program for senior citizens and
November 28, 1979

single parent families; a special assistance program for needy families to compensate for rising heating and electricity costs; a temporary reduction in interest rates paid by home owners who must renegotiate their mortgage-this is one of the major problems which this proposal does not answer adequately- assistance programs for buyers of new homes to stimulate the housing industry; and last, subsidies for the construction of rental units in metropolitan areas where the occupancy rate is very low.
Mr. Speaker, those are five proposals put forward by the official housing critic of the Liberal party, which in my opinion deal much more adequately with the present housing problems in Canada than that weird proposal by the Progressive Conservative government, a proposal which is a remnant of some hasty electoral promises put together and in a way forcing the Progressive Conservative government to act.
This government has had to beat a retreat on its promise to move the Canadian embassy from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem. They are now looking for a compromise in order not to carry out their promise about Petro-Canada. They have already changed in part their general mortgage interest deductibility proposal. They have changed a very large part of the deductibility project to make it a tax credit. It is an important part already of that promise that has been changed. If the Progressive Conservatives are conscientious and courageous, they should recognize their error in this area as in others. What is called for is not a slight alteration in the promise, but outright recognition that the proposal does not meet the needs. The minister in charge of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation should be given an opportunity to put forward a genuine policy meeting Canada's housing needs, a policy that would indeed fill the needs of those who would like to have their own home, those who have an uncertain view of the future because of the astronomical increase in the interest rates, those who could get no better promise than the assurance that, were they to buy a house, they would not be charged interest rates higher than a given figure throughout the repayment period. Therefore the government could implement a program of so-called shelter allowance, a housing supplement assistance program that would help both rental dwellers and home owners keep housing costs in Canada at an acceptable level.
I am thinking of a system that could help rental dwellers by allowing them to deduct from their income tax rental costs above a certain proportion of their income, say 25 per cent, and also a program that could help home owners through income tax deduction of housing costs incurred in the form of mortgage interests, property taxes, heating costs and insurance premiums, also at that 25 per cent of income level. I feel that any sensible policy helping not only the residential housing industry in Canada but also giving confidence to any Canadian wanting to own his or her own house would be to establish a system under which the individual would know in advance that he or she would not be confronted three, four or five years
Mortgage Tax Credit
hence with excessive extra costs that cannot be met. It is a matter of common sense, therefore, that the Minister of Finance in no way satisfies the people's needs with this camouflaged proposal. All he is doing is giving some sort of income tax rebate to a privileged few. 1 have no objection to the Minister of Finance granting tax benefits to some Canadians, whether it be $375 this year or $750 next year. If he wants to let some Canadians pay less income tax, that is his privilege. But I do have serious objections to the fact that the Minister of Finance uses this technique to lower the income tax of certain people, not of all Canadian taxpayers, that he does not act frankly and unequivocally for everybody. If he wants to lower taxes, that is fine, but he should not, by the back door and underhandedly, try to favour a privileged few and at the same time try to convince us that what he is proposing is an adequate policy for solving Canada's housing problems.
In my view, that is just not good enough. Such a measure prevents the implementation of a real housing policy. It is unacceptable and inadequate, and it is something that we are subjected to only because the leader of the government, the leader of the Progressive Conservative Party, has made unacceptable election promises to gain a few votes in towns and suburbs around large Canadian cities. That is not worthy of the leader of a government. Now that he is Prime Minister of this country, he should be honest enough to recognize, as he did in the case of the embassy move to Jerusalem, that he made a mistake; and in this case, that he will amend the act and ask the minister responsible for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to introduce real amendments that will help solve the real housing problems in Canada. Then we shall be very happy to support an over-all housing policy in Canada, which should serve well not only a few privileged home owners who live in certain areas of the country but all Canadians, in all parts of the country, and benefit them whether they are owners or tenants, whether they live in cities or in rural areas; then we shall be only too happy to support the government, if it has the courage to do what it must.
But if it persists in pursuing this silly short-term policy, we will have no choice but to denounce it and say that this is horse trading, that this is a shameful policy, that we condemn this way of managing the affairs of the state, of squandering the taxpayers' money, of wasting it to favour only a few of the already privileged to the detriment of thousands of Canadians who are in need, really in need, of decent housing, at a reasonable price, and whom the Progressive Conservative Party completely ignores, for it is heartless: it has nothing but political debts.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TAX CREDIT IN RESPECT OF MORTGAGE INTEREST AND PROPERTY TAX
speechtext:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has said that it is not December yet, but nonetheless that is the date on the questionnaire.
One of the questions in the questionnaire is:
Do you think mortgage interest should be deductible from taxable income?
The number of respondents who said yes to that question amounted to 60 per cent of the people who replied.
Other questionnaires conducted by other members of this party and parties on all sides of the House have indicated quite clearly that the Canadian people accept, as a beginning to a range of home owner benefits, the proposal for a property tax credit advanced by this party. That is what is concerning the Liberal party, Mr. Speaker. It is why the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) said it was an exceedingly important bill for this government with respect to its commitments to the Canadian people.
We can find quotations to support both sides of this issue. There are economists and public commentators who have said the bill is unwise; there are an equal number of economists and public commentators who have said it is at least a worth-while experiment, and there are others who go beyond that and say it is a wise move and a good beginning to a legislative program that will help home owners. There are economists on all sides of the issue, but economists and tax experts do not make up the majority of the Canadian people.
I should like to recount an experience during the election campaign as 1 went door to door in a single family area of my
Mortgage Tax Credit
riding, known as Briargreen. As we were going up the street a man ran out of his house and greeted us. He said he was in the midst of making out his income tax return and, Mr. Speaker, he was furious. I was very happy at that point to be a member of the opposition rather than a member of the government. He had read about the property tax credit and the mortgage deductibility scheme. He said, "Mr. Baker, does your party mean to do this?" I replied, "Yes, we do. You can count on it." If that gentleman is listening, or if he reads Hansard, I should like to tell him that this bill is the answer to his question. We intend to deal with this piece of legislation.
There are some people who say this bill will not benefit people who live in apartments. That is right. Many people who would like to have a choice of housing are denied that choice because of a whole host of things, many of which are far beyond the control of government. Other people live in apartments because they like them, although many choose to move out of apartments if they can.
This bill will provide encouragement to the construction industry. It is not the end of the encouragement that can be provided, but it shows that the government cares about the proposition of home ownership as a beginning with respect to construction, leading ultimately to the shelter tax that everyone talks about. Who in this House will condemn the beginning of some relief for home owners? That is the issue, Mr. Speaker. No one on this side of the House has said that this bill constitutes the last word with respect to the alleviation of the problems of home ownership. It is one of the steps toward that end, and I ask my friends on all sides of the House to consider it from that point of view. I think this is important.
The hon. member for Papineau said that high interest rates in Canada make this proposition, and the government's approach, useless. Mr. Speaker, I think this makes it more relevant. How can anyone argue, when interest rates are rising, that anything designed to alleviate high interest rates is not important? When municipal taxes are rising, how can anyone argue that some alleviation is not important? I think it is becoming more relevant all the time.
In answer to questions in this House, the Minister of Finance has said he thinks that in the long run interest rates will come down. That is already evident in the mortgage market. If one accepts even part of the argument of the hon. member for Papineau, it is clear that as mortgage interest rates come down, this bill will have a greater effect.
This party did not choose the property tax approach by accident, Mr. Speaker. Hon. members on all sides of the House recognize the difficulty of dealing with the provinces in this matter. The property tax credit was the only way to deal with them. This method was chosen because it has impact on people in the lower income brackets to a greater degree than on people in the higher income bracket. I suppose that is why the Gallup poll has indicated that about 70 per cent of Canadians are behind the scheme. The poll does not discriminate between apartment dwellers and home owners. Colleagues of mine have received 80 per cent and 90 per cent returns in favour of the proposition. The hon. member for

November 28, 1979
Mortgage Tax Credit
Vancouver Centre found that 60 per cent of those replying thought it was a good proposition and worthy of support.
This is the first time that the tax system of the country has been used to give some relief to this segment of the community. There are a great number of programs for those who are disadvantaged. Indeed, I think this country is in the lead in programs for the disadvantaged. The really wealthy do not need programs in the way that the disadvantaged do. There is a group of Canadians who traditionally have borne a large portion of the cost for such programs, and that is middle income Canadians. As wages improve and the differential between wage groups and occupations decreases, that group is growing in number.
I hope there is no one in this House who will vote against this bill which is a first step toward relief of property taxes. The hon. member for Papineau referred to the statement of the minister responsible for housing, to the effect that we are working toward a shelter allowance. Of course we are. There would be a shelter allowance already but the fact is we do not have the fiscal stability to put this in place nor are we likely to have it for some time. But this is the first step in that direction. Surely to goodness no one in this House will vote against it. If they do, they are flying in the face of the opinion of most Canadians.
I want to address another aspect of the bill, Mr. Speaker, relating to my responsibility as Minister of National Revenue. It is up to the House whether this bill is passed, and this is a minority House. The bill would be administered by my department, and I should like to address certain technical aspects of the implementation of the program so that members on all sides of the House will know the position in which the government is placed.
A short time ago my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggested, almost in an aside, that the government may already have printed the tax forms even though the debate had not begun. I want to tell the House that my hon. friend was quite correct, and I want to tell the House why. He has been here for a long time and he knew he was right when he put the question in the aside.
I do think it is appropriate that I leave the impression that the forms with respect to the property tax credit are ready, and had to be so. I want to tell members why that is the case so that they will understand. Canadian taxpayers will be receiving a form in a relatively few days which will contain the property tax credit deduction lines. I want to tell them as well so that they know about some innovations with respect to the form. As a result of the work of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Crombie), the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Grafftey), in his former capacity as minister of state for social programs, and officials of my department, there is a simplified approach in the general form to the child tax credit provision. We hope that we will not run into problems that ail members have experienced with respect to the last matter in terms of the printing that has to be done.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TAX CREDIT IN RESPECT OF MORTGAGE INTEREST AND PROPERTY TAX
speechtext:
Perhaps I could answer that question best by continuing my speech. If the hon. member is not satisfied with what occurs in it, he will see the position that we are in now.
Hon. members opposite made a picture of a printing press at the ready to incorporate their amendments into a new tax form to run off the returns the moment this bill has been given royal assent. They may suggest, since they have clearly declared their intention not to pass Bill C-20, that no returns should be mailed out. I anxiously await the pleasure of the House with respect to the bill, quite naturally, because my department will be administering it. Unfortunately, I cannot await the pleasure of the House with respect to the forms.
In a normal taxation year, labelling and enveloping of returns would start on October 8 and be delivered to the Post Office with mailing to be completed by the end of December. Processing of these returns would begin in early February, and refund cheques would begin to go out at that time. As a department our peak activity happens to be around mid-March.
There have been delays this year because a form had to be designed for a mortgage interest and property tax schedule. It had to be redesigned, printed and enveloped with the return. As well, the main form had to include a reference to that schedule so that the taxpayer, when he receives it, will receive a form that has the lines and the reference to the schedule to assist him in preparing the property tax credit aspect of that form. Therefore, this year enveloping started about November 21-not a significant delay having regard to the problems- and mailing must take place at the beginning of next week if delays are not built up. As the matter stands right now, refund cheques will be two weeks later than usual. If there is a delay in getting this bill through parliament, that refund period will be put back even further.
1 should give my friends in the House some indication of the volume that we are talking about. The printing of the tax forms is a huge task; it is a monumental task. There are 15 million packages now prepared, each one containing a label, a pre-addressed tax form containing a tax guide, a separate property tax schedule, and a return envelope. In addition to this, other forms must be made available through post offices across the country.
We gave consideration to the possibility of delaying the mailing of the forms until Bill C-20 passed, in case it did not pass. I want to tell the House that we gave consideration in the department to that. Recognizing that the bill might not pass,
November 28, 1979

we felt that in the interests of all taxpayers we could not introduce a long delay in the tax return cycle. Such a delay would be hard not only to those planning to apply for the new deductions, but also to all taxpayers.
This past year 11,370,000 refunds were issued for a total of $4.5 billion. Not all these refunds went to taxpayers in the strictest sense because these returns are sent in as part of the various income maintenance schemes across the country, both nationally and provincially. For example, in the federal child tax credit scheme there are about 800,000 of those. Then there is the Ontario property sales and pensioners' tax credits, the Manitoba cost of living and property tax credit, the Alberta rental assistance credit, the British Columbia rental tax credit, and a shelter tax credit in the province of Saskatchewan. The delay of the refunds would cause hardship for thousands of people for whom a refund is more than just a spring bonus.
I do not have to tell any member of this House how important is the child tax credit to many single parents. I do not have to tell any member of this House how important and how significant a delay can be. Therefore, as a government, we really had no alternative. In all probability, the April 30 deadline would have had to be extended. In some cases, some loss of income might result. Even if a delay in mailing the forms took place, the government would have been unable to do little if Bill C-20 were to be defeated by whatever means. The opening and restuffing of 15 million envelopes, or the reprinting of certain lines in the returns, is just not a practical alternative. For all of these reasons, the government has little choice but to mail the tax forms, and this will be done, as 1 have indicated, in the very near future.
Hon. members are probably aware that this has been done before in anticipation of eventual passage. Clearly the present situation with a minority government is different. I want to tell the House that by ordering the forms to be sent, I am not presuming passage of the bill. That does not lie with my department or me, it lies with members of this House of Commons. In fact, I have listened to and read speeches of hon. members opposite. Their determination not to pass the bill is quite evident. I felt, quite frankly, that I ought to come to the House and indicate to my colleagues on all sides of the House the situation and the circumstances behind it.
This obviously raises the question: what happens if the opposition is denying the tax deduction to the people of Canada, at least for the year 1979? I think the Minister of Finance made it clear, and we have made it clear, that we want this bill. The whole purpose of this bill is to apply it to the taxes of ratepayers, property owners, for the year 1979, which would be utilized by them in the spring of 1980 when they file their tax returns for 1979.
If there is a delay, that would require the Department of National Revenue to do several things. First, we would have to launch a publicity campaign telling the taxpayers to ignore the mortgage interest and property tax schedule. Quite frankly, I would regret this since the government is trying to cut back on advertising. I would say to you that we would not want to be flooded with several million returns claiming a deduction
Mortgage Tax Credit
which is just not there. So we would have no alternative but to embark on an advertising compaign. From my brief experience as Minister of National Revenue 1 can safely predict that an endless stream of correspondence about a tax deduction that never came about would have to be answered by me as the departmental minister responsible-and I would certainly answer all this correspondence truthfully, as hon. members would expect me to do.
Second, we would program the computer to ignore this particular deduction should it be claimed, and I predict that computers would be just as unpopular as would be the House of Commons, in particular some hon. members who are sitting over there on the other side.
I have to tell the House that the sending of the forms early next week arises from necessity and normal practice, and in no way denies the House the right to make a decision on this matter. If the opposition decides to defeat this measure I hope members over there will understand the need to conduct an advertizing campaign to prevent a build-up at taxation data centres of several million erroneous returns. I felt that in advance of a question period in the spring of 1980 1 should tell hon. members that right now. I am hopeful, of course, that the opposition will not deny this tax advantage to home owners in Canada.
I do not see anything wrong, in fact, I see a great deal that is right, in encouraging home ownership. Ownership of a home is a provision for the present and a protection for the future. Home ownership is not an unnatural desire among Canadians and it behoves the government, within the limits of its ability financially in any one year, to promote it.
This is the first step in a program which attempts to assist toward reaching a goal which we consider desirable, that is, home ownership, by at least giving the option, the choice, to Canadians. It is not just Canadians in the large cities, it is not just Canadians who live in apartments in large cities; it is Canadians who live on farms, Canadians who live in small towns and hamlets, Canadians everywhere who want the choice. They will have the benefits of this bill. However imperfect it may seem to be, that is the choice this government wants to begin to give. It was announced a long time ago. I think ownership of a home is a very tangible expression of accomplishment and of a commitment to community. It is an expression of it only; it is not a commitment but it is an expression of it and we think it is an expression worth fostering.
With respect to the amendment the hon. gentleman talked about, let me say this. He knows there are limitations which govern the moving of amendments, limitations under the rules with respect to the amending of tax bills. And they would apply to the bill before us. The Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) indicated we were prepared to consider amendments. But I would have to say that to amend this scheme this year would so foul it up from the administration point of view as to render the whole process of this first step difficult. Indeed, in terms of

November 28, 1979
Mortgage Tax Credit
delay, it could become meaningless. 1 see no way by which we could amend this scheme today to bring in the shelter tax allowance scheme, if that is the kind of amendment members over there are talking about-I see the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) nodding his head. Physically, it could not be done.
1 want to say to the hon. member that he ought to regard this as a first step in a number of steps. The government is not unmindful of the reasonable comments which have be made with respect to the importance of the shelter tax allowance. I want to tell hon. members that through you, Mr. Speaker. But for the year 1979, both in terms of the ability of the government to pay and in the physical ability of the government to allow, it is just not feasible. There may be other amendments we can consider but they would have to be quite minor. I regret having to put that as being the position of the government, and I do so from the point of view of my responsibilities as Minister of National Revenue.
I am sure all hon. members, knowing the background of the Minister of Finance and knowing the concern he has for people and the fairness of the tax system, understand he would want to do everything he could with respect to the tax system if that was allowed to him. But the government is under certain constraints financially and that is not possible this year. 1 would not say it would not be possible in other years, nor do I say the government would not consider it in other years. As the hon. member for Papineau indicated in his speech, the minister responsible for housing is quoted as saying the government does have this matter under review. And, of course, it does. But this is a first step and, as a first step, I ask members in all quarters of the House to support it recognizing, as I do, the differences of opinion which may exist philosophically.
That is the reason I got into this debate, Mr. Speaker. 1 felt it was quite important that all members of the House of Commons should understand the unavoidable problems of the Department of National Revenue with respect to the preparation of the forms and the problems which will result to the Canadian taxpayer in the event that this bill is defeated. I really felt it would be unfair if that point was not made by me. Quite frankly, if I can, I want to avoid questions in the spring of 1980, if this bill is defeated, by telling the House in advance what the problems are-questions related to the delay in returns and these other matters. 1 want to thank hon. members for their attention.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few comments to make in this debate before its conclusion and the calling of the vote, which the hon. minister has indicated he is looking forward to with such anxiety.
I was concerned when the minister who has just spoken indicated that one of the reasons, in his view, that this government is called upon to take the step it is taking now to assist home owners, about which he claims such great anxiety, is that municipal taxes are going up. Although that particular concern may be laudable in itself, I have grave concern that what he is attempting to do is draw the whole federal system into a
Mortgage Tax Credit
debate from time to time and on an annual basis with municipalities and municipal taxpayers as to whether or not the federal government should be called upon, on an annual basis, to come to the aid of municipal taxpayers every year and each time taxes go up, as an opportunity for the federal government to provide, via some side door if not the back door, more assistance to municipalities through this kind of tax credit system. I cannot believe we are getting ourselves into a system which would see the federal jurisdiction trying to provide funds, in effect, for the payment of municipal taxes.
I cannot believe the naivete which would lead us into a position where municipalities would be asking on an annual basis for increases in this kind of assistance which would properly reflect the increases in taxes and mill rates going on in all of the townships, towns, villages and cities in this country. I am concerned about what the true basis for moving forward with this kind of legislation might be.
The minister also said that he has grave concern about, and interest in, providing reasonable relief for some segment, and that he could not understand that the hon. member for Papi-neau (Mr. Ouellet) would call this a waste. The fact that there is some assistance given is not in itself a waste, but it is a waste when we are dealing with a limited resource and when we cannot conceive of trying to priorize that resource and put it where it is most valuable and most needed. All of us individually, let alone with the assistance of the ministries behind the various government ministers, should be able to tell this government and itemize for this government a number of priorities which, all hon. members could agree, surely must come in advance of providing assistance to middle-income house owners, so-called, who seem to be targeted by this piece of legislation.
The minister asked that someone in authority give some indication as to where the vote is going. Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party believes that every Canadian has the right to decent housing at prices he or she can afford. I hope there is no person in this House, or any member who is not in the House, who would disagree with that as a legitimate goal for Canada.
The economic arguments for and against Bill C-20 have been covered in depth by a number of previous speakers, the most outstanding of whom was my colleague, the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae). Therefore, I want to consider right now the effect the mortgage credit scheme would have in relation to some of the practical housing realities which face ordinary people. I would like to use the city of Vancouver as an example. I think it is probably typical of many things facing other urban centres.

We cannot consider mortgage tax credits which benefit so few people and cost so much without first looking at urban housing and rural housing needs, housing alternatives, and government assistance programs which are absolutely essential to meet the needs of so many people. In Vancouver we recently did a study of some 160,000 households. Of course that includes a great many more people. The study indicated that 45 per cent of these households are people who own their own homes, some of them with mortgages which they are paying off, and that 55 per cent of the households are occupied by tenants. Unfortunately, only 1 per cent of these households are co-operative housing units, those having been built very recently. There is a vacancy rate in Vancouver of .2 per cent; two-tenths of 1 per cent, and that is quite unheard of in our recent history. You can see from this that we need housing desperately. There are precious few places for people to go.
Average rents as listed in classified ads are up to about $450. Surely I do not have to ask hon. members in this House why housing is so tight in this and in other cities. If that is not the case, then why are tenants not moving out and purchasing their own homes? It is obvious to anyone who looks at costs today that they cannot afford houses, and it is ridiculous to think that a tax credit such as is being proposed today can assist in this regard. Not even the tax credit system, the carrot that is being promised for next year and for following years, will help solve this problem. Because of high interest rates we know that home ownership is just simply not an option for most of our cities' renters.
Let us take a look at housing costs in relation to the incomes of people, and again this is in Vancouver, but I am sure it is relevant to other parts of Canada. About 10 per cent of Vancouver residents spend more than 50 per cent of their incomes on housing, and again most of these people are renting. Anyone who knows anything at all about housing knows that the CMHC and every housing authority suggest that we must not allow people to spend more than 25 per cent or, at the most, 35 per cent of their incomes on housing. Most renters in Vancouver cannot afford to buy housing since you must earn over $22,000 at least to consider a mortgage these days. At today's rates of interest we know how much of that additional money will be needed to pay off interest rates in the future.
There are 7 per cent of renters in Vancouver who earn over $22,000, however, and many of those people choose to live in rented accommodation. They choose to be tenants. However, I would like to point out to our friends across the way, since many of these people earning over $22,000 supposedly voted for them, that these are the people they are asking to pay the cost of tax credits for an elite and small group of people who will be lucky enough to be in homes paying off mortgages this year. Those are the people who will have to pay a large chunk of the cost of this program through their own income tax payments.
November 28, 1979

Over one quarter of the householders in Vancouver, or about 40,000 families, must spend well over 30 per cent of their incomes on housing. I know many of these people, and I know for sure that this means that in order to pay that proportion of their income for housing they will have to take it out of food budgets, and that means less nourishing food for children.
Approximately 22 per cent of the households that we looked at are occupied by senior citizens, and at least half of those own their own houses, the other half being renters. Of the elderly renters, of course, many are senior citizens on fixed incomes, and with the exception of those who are lucky enough to live in government assisted housing, they spend in excess of 30 per cent of their incomes on housing. These are people on pensions who have no opportunity of having a COLA clause in their incomes each year. Surely they also deserve a tax credit, just as much as do home owners.
In Vancouver close to 40 per cent of our elderly citizens have worked very hard throughout their lives to pay off their mortgages, and their homes are very important to them. They own their homes outright. How do you think they feel about having to pay for the benefits of a tax credit system that will only benefit such a few? It seems to me that they are also people who are being penalized for working, saving, raising their families, and buying homes over the years.
Another 35 per cent of our home owners who are in their middle years have also paid off their homes in Vancouver. They have raised their kids; their kids are probably teenagers or even young adults, many of them living at home still because they cannot find jobs. They will also have to pay through their income tax for this tax credit being given to people who are paying for their own homes through the mortgage system.
I also want to mention tenants particularly. The majority of people in Vancouver are tenants, as is probably the case in most urban centres today. Tenants are facing an extremely serious situation because of the lack of vacancies and the income situation which is not producing more housing for the people. Again this relates back to today's high interest rates.
We are finding in Vancouver now that rent controls are just being applied in a very few cases and rents are skyrocketing. 1 was speaking to one of the handicapped women who was here the other day. She told me she expects rent controls to be removed and that rents will go up over 30 per cent. With the incomes of the handicapped and others, they simply cannot afford this.
The poor people, particularly tenants who have children, many of them single parents raising families and having a difficult time of it, have absolutely no chance to live anywhere else. They do not even dare consider looking for other places of accommodation. They are at the mercy of their landlords. Incidentally, many of these are the same landlords to whom the Liberal government gave very generous tax credits, through tax shelters and incentives, and they are not now passing on the benefits to their tenants.
Mortgage Tax Credit
I would now like to consider the ordinary working person who is typical of the people in my riding of Vancouver East, and I am sure typical of other ridings across the country as well. An average worker who is lucky enough to have a year-round job in our area earns between $13,000 and $15,000 a year. Obviously, not one of these workers on his own can purchase a home. That is why, of course, so many of the wives of male workers must also consider working. It is usually the wife who is working at menial jobs with low rates of pay, and who now has no right to unemployment insurance if she can only find a part-time job. These wives have to work to support their families, and hopefully to save a little bit toward a down payment to get a home eventually. This is what many families want. Unfortunately, the increasing cost of fuel, food, clothing and transportation uses up every dollar in the pay cheque. Even with two parents working, very few are saving these days. The disposable income for working people in Vancouver dropped 3 per cent last year.
It is ridiculous for the members of the Conservative party who have produced this bill to say that the dream of owning a home will be fulfilled for young people today. That is absolute garbage. There is no way the dream of owning a home will be realized, and it is fast fading in the minds of most young people today.
Let me give one example of Mr. Dan Jones, a small businessman, who earns about $15,000 average per year. He is lucky to have a business, and with present policies I do not know how much longer his business will survive. His wife worked for a while and helped to save $7,000. They have one child and are expecting a second. They are very keen to get into a house of their own. They found a three-bedroom house in Vancouver East at the modest price of $65,000. That is a pretty good price for today. The lot size was 33 feet.
These people saved enough to make a down payment of $7,000, leaving a $58,000 mortgage. It does not sound like very much, and surely the average working person could afford such a home. But if we consider interest rates of up to 14 per cent, this couple would pay over the next 30 years $300,000 in interest alone. The taxes would be $400 a year and, of course, their fuel costs will be up this winter. These people concluded that if they were to buy this house they would pay at least $755 a month, which amounts to 50 per cent of their income. Of course there is no way that they could buy this house.
I ask hon. gentlemen and the hon. woman member as well, what good is a tax credit of $375 a year as an incentive for getting people into housing when the average working person, who has a family with two kids and a modest home, needs this much to subsidize the rent because of high interest rates? There is no way that a young family can get into a house in the first place, so what good is this tax credit to them? It is hypocritical to say that this program will help young families get into houses.
What young people need is a bill that will help reduce their monthly payment to 25 per cent or 35 per cent of their income.

The government could do this by reducing bank profits, by reducing interest rates, by providing subsidies on interest rates, or by building decent social housing and directly using the taxpayers' money, rather than giving it to the banks. A previous speaker opposite has said that this mortgage tax credit bill will encourage home ownership. That is a delusion. I am very insulted and angry that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) deceived this House when he said, I felt, in a very sarcastic way, that the mortgage tax credit would encourage young people to purchase a home, live a good life and raise a family. The minister has simply not looked at the facts. Why is he raising the hopes of people? Is he a cynic or a sadist?
