speechtext:
To me it is cynicism and sadism to deceive people by promising them this tax credit, which was nothing more than a gimmick to get votes. It leads people to think that they will now be able to purchase a home.
The manager of the mortgage department of Canada Trust in Vancouver, who is a supporter of the Conservative party, has said, "High mortgage interest rates have made the hoped-for benefits from Ottawa's mortgage interest deductibility plan an exercise in futility". Lending institutions have also said that there has been a pronounced drop-off in housing business stocks in late October and that it has continued into November. Certainly it will continue into the new year.
Many of my constituents will appreciate a mortgage tax credit, even though it will hardly meet the increased costs of their fuel. On the other hand, they will lose money when the children's allowance benefits are taken away. I am thinking particularly of families who have just come to Canada, and who have struggled to save for down payments to purchase, in most cases, older homes. These people have worked very hard to improve their homes and have rented out parts of their homes to help pay for the mortgage. We must also consider that these people have probably sponsored their grandparents and other members of the family to come to Canada to share their home, thus there are often several wage earners who can contribute. If anyone deserves a tax credit, 1 would say that these people do.
Many working people and trade union members who are earning decent salaries and paying for mortgages will not say no to this tax credit plan. They, too, need this subsidy, because in more and more families the children are staying at home into their young adult years because they are unable to find jobs. These young people are faced with ever increasing costs and the prospect of not finding work. Should they be so lucky as to find work, their wages will probably not keep abreast of the increasing cost of living.
We in the New Democratic Party do not object to these families receiving such a tax credit because it will help cover exorbitant interest rates and the high cost of living of today. However, I am sure that my constituents would agree that we

must be fair, and we know that renters, and young families who are unable to afford a home, would also like a tax credit.
There are many forms of social housing. When talking about affordable housing, this is an essential consideration. For example, a good alternative would be housing co-operatives. With some adjustments to the present system and an increase in monetary support to develop such housing, we could meet the needs of many young families today. Co-operative housing requires a small down payment because the mortgage is taken out collectively. Many of the housing cooperatives in Vancouver have been built on leased land. There is not a huge profit for developers in this form of housing, and as a result the costs are lower. Such a program would provide decent, attractive, family housing in livable communities.
The scheme in British Columbia is based on the concept that this housing will provide mixed, self-reliant communities. Surely that is a program which the government could support. Financially speaking, these housing communities contain average wage earners, 70 per cent; those slightly above the average income of $15,000, 20 per cent; and those below the average income, 10 per cent. Because these people collectively live together, they can meet their costs collectively. These people pay only 25 per cent to 30 per cent of their income toward the mortgage. This is the kind of housing in which the government should invest. If the Conservative party is committed to young families who want to own their own homes, it should provide this kind of housing.
Having talked to many groups in Vancouver and to CMHC officials, I have learned that the amount of money allocated for social housing is being used primarily to pay interest rates to the banks. This money is not being spent on housing. In fact there is very little money left for this year for starting new housing developments. Even in cases where the federal program-and I think that it is a good program-subsidizes interest rates to the point where people are paying 2 per cent for non-profit housing, the subsidy is being paid to the banks in the form of interest.
Another program which the government should continue to support, but unfortunately 1 do not think there will be any money this year for expansion, is social housing for senior citizens. There are many developments of this nature in many communities across Canada. It is excellent housing and the senior citizens are happy with it. Every year there is an increasing number of elderly people who will be needing this type of housing. Already there are long waiting lists, but no money to put into new developments of this kind. Senior citizens and other people living in subsidized housing are helping to pay for this tax credit to home owners. Even the non-profit groups that supposedly want to build housing for senior citizens receive no tax incentives such as are proposed in Bill C-20.
Public housing in Canada is at a standstill. I have known and worked in huge public housing ghettos in Vancouver such as Skeena, McLean Park and Raymur. That is not the kind of
November 28, 1979

public housing that we need, as I am sure everyone would agree. What we need is the type of housing that will integrate with communities and allow people to move out of rat-infested dwellings and pay a rent that is 25 per cent of their income. But no public housing is being built.
Under our system, poor people themselves pay the operating costs and capital costs of public housing when they live in it. It is said to be highly subsidized, but actually it is not. The government has actually subsidized the banks. The government is financing the profits and the interest rate, which is three quarters of the cost of the project, and government authorities are the ones that are paying that to the banks. If tax money were used directly for housing, more money could be saved and put into expanded housing programs. Non-profit housing programs for families are at a complete standstill. There are many plans on the books, such as the plan for the Strathcona community in Vancouver. This would provide excellent housing in the downtown area but it will probably not come to fruition unless there is considerable change in federal policy. The tax credit system will not help to meet that goal.
Just yesterday the hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle) spoke in very emotional terms about housing in Third World countries. I share his concerns in this area, but in downtown Vancouver, in the skid row area, there is a third world country that is worse than many of those overseas. Year after year people live in rat-infested and cockroach-infested rooms. Most of the houses are owned by landlords who have ripped off the tax system and have not put anything into improving the housing. Most of the tenants do not have a place to eat where they live. Often there is a dirty washroom, a couple of floors down, which must be shared. The buildings are fire traps, but these people cannot get out of this type of housing.
There are many single people, and couples and immigrants, living in this way. Incidentally, many of the Vietnamese refugees are being forced to live in this way as well. They are competing with * the poor for this terrible housing. Native people coming in from the reserves are being forced to live in this terrible housing, or even on the streets. I would particularly like to mention many single and middle-aged women who cannot get into public housing because they have no children. Women are desperately short of housing.
The program being proposed to subsidize mortgages would do nothing to solve the housing problem for the people I have mentioned. A self-help organization in this area, the Downtown Residents Association, has been fighting for years to get something done. They have developed plans for housing but are fed up with the red tape and buck-passing they encounter at every level of government. It is my opinion that under this government, and with the present federal programs, there is no way they will ever get housing in the downtown area. Why should we not be taking the money to help those people, if we have a priority, rather than the people who already have had enough money to get their own houses? This is only a drop in the bucket for them anyway as far as mortgage costs are concerned.
Mortgage Tax Credit
We must address the question of how we pay for social housing. I have already mentioned that most of the federal housing money, which comes out of your pocket and mine through income tax, is going to the banks and not to housing. The government is going to privatize CMHC, if it has not done so already. This means that the total financing will be turned over to the private sector.
The only way we can assure low and middle income people of a decent place to live is through government sponsored housing and co-operatives, and non-profit housing developments, financed by the government, using our tax dollars directly for housing, rather than going through the banks and paying most of the money into bank profits. Through conversations with people at CMHC I know that the allocation of funds for housing, even if they were not paying most of it out in interest, is not enough to make new starts this year.
I do not want to go into any more of the history of this, Mr. Speaker. Since 1967 there has been a dramatic change and the system has been completely switched around. Maybe we should look at the pre-1967 government housing policy, where the money allocated for housing went directly into housing starts.
The policy of both Tories and Liberals is to allow the banks to take over-to bleed profits from the taxpayers' money while government cuts back on the amount of money budgeted for social housing. I have spoken about many non-profit alternatives, Mr. Speaker, which surely must be considered as a priority for the limited dollars available for housing starts in Canada. Of course we would like to see tax credits for home owners in middle income brackets, but not at the expense of other Canadians who have just as much right to decent, affordable housing.
Let us ask tenants if they are willing to pay out of their income tax, or to give up subsidies for housing that they should have, in order to provide mortgage tax credits for the elite few who are in housing now and are paying off their mortgages. Let us ask home owners who have worked very hard, particularly senior citizens who have worked hard to pay off their homes, and see if they are content to have social programs cut and, if they pay income tax, to subsidize a privileged few.
If this government wants to buy votes with a Christmas bonus, I challenge them to pay a tax credit fairly and universally to all Canadians. If we are going to do it for one small group, why not do it for everybody?
I should like to conclude by summarizing what the New Democratic Party would do if it were the government, and I would seriously urge this government to consider these measures in a non-partisan way, as being very important to the direction Canada should go. We would make housing for all Canadians, not just an elite few, a No. 1 priority. We would reduce interest rates, particularly for Canadians who earn under $30,000 or $35,000. This would really help young families, in particular, to purchase a home. We would not pay billions of dollars in interest, which is increasing every year, to enrich the banks. Instead, we would use this money to build housing. We would create jobs. We would provide incentives

November 28, 1979
Mortgage Tax Credit
for co-operatives. We would provide incentives for new communities, and particularly for young families who would flourish and improve our land.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TAX CREDIT IN RESPECT OF MORTGAGE INTEREST AND PROPERTY TAX
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TAX CREDIT IN RESPECT OF MORTGAGE INTEREST AND PROPERTY TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am very pleased to be able to rise in this debate on Bill C-20. To me, this bill is hardly acceptable in its present form for many reasons, and 1 intend to be as objective as I can in this speech and prove indeed how extravagant, irresponsible and unfair this piece of legislation is.

This bill which has been placed before us today has quite a history. The Prime Minister (Mr. Clark) enumerated deductibility of mortgage interest as his major election platform over a year ago, in September, 1978. We Liberals in government at that time opposed his scheme as fiscally irresponsible, wasteful and unfair. Despite the changes made largely through pressure from our party and many commentators from across Canada, to the Prime Minister's original proposal, the basic philosophy of the bill remains just that. It is fiscally irresponsible, because in a difficult economic period and a time of restraint this government has committed itself to extra billions of dollars of expenditures, $2.87 billion by its own "conservative" estimate by 1982. Goodness knows how much more after that.
It is ironic that the government which has committed itself to reducing government expenditures, cutting back the public service, privatizing everything it sees, is making such an irresponsible, open-ended financial commitment. Moreover, this government has been following a high interest rate policy which will virtually negate any benefits that its tax credit will give to Canadians.
I am sure hon. members have read comments printed in The Financial Times of Canada. What does the real estate industry have to say? An article in the Ottawa Citizen dated October 18, 1979, pointed out the following:
Ottawa realtors say if the federal government is genuinely concerned about home ownership in Canada then they should do something about record high interest rates instead of introducing mortgage tax credits. "It's a gimmick, let's face it, it's a gimick," said George Coughlan, manager of Shipman Real Estate's centre town office.
The industry sees this plan for what it really is, not a housing policy, not even a fiscal policy, but an election gimmick.

And Mr. Yvan Guay wrote as follows in the daily La Presse, on September 19, 1979:
The Canadian people must therefore ask themselves whether that reduction in tax revenue will be offset by an increase in tax revenue resulting from the new jobs a stimulated building industry will create. Otherwise, the federal government will have to reduce more or less its services to the public. Considering the price of city lots, construction costs, property taxes and mortgage interest rates, all of which are constantly rising, one cannot see how this tax credit could be enough to promote residential construction.

Moreover, as pointed out in The Globe and Mail for October 26, 1979:

-about 874,000 Canadian families have lost the ability to qualify for a $60,000 five-year term mortgage amortized over twenty-five years on a $66,000 home because of the rapid escalation in mortgage rates this year.
The article went on to demonstrate that with this mortgage interest rate rise to 14.75 per cent and even higher, a home owner would have to pay $736.81 per month on such a $60,000 mortgage on a $66,000 house when, at the beginning of the year with interest rates at 10.5 per cent, that home owner would have paid $557 per month. That is an extra $179.81 per month, or $2,157.72 per year. And yet this Conservative government thinks that if it gives home owners, those who fully qualify for both the mortgage interest and property tax credits, $375, people will buy homes and thus will stimulate the housing market. That is just crazy. The home owner we have just spoken of will still be out $1,782.72 since the beginning of this year.

In an article which appeared in the November 9, 1978, issue of Le Devoir, Statistics Canada stated, and I quote:
Nearly half of the some 4.8 million home owners in Canada would benefit little or not at all from the mortgage tax credits which the Conservative government has announced, on the basis of the most recent figures from Statistics Canada.
Only some 16 per cent or 17 per cent of Canadians will benefit from this program.

That is just the tip of the iceberg. Since this government took power in June of this year, the cost of living and operating a home has simply soared. In only five months to October of this year, the rate of inflation has risen from 8.9 per cent to 9.3 per cent. The consumer price index has risen 2.8 per cent. The construction material index has risen 3.7 per cent. The residential building input price index has risen by 2.4 per cent, and the cost of regular unleaded gasoline has risen 12 per cent per litre. This will go higher when we know what agreement the Prime Minister has reached with the Premier of Alberta.
In the five-month period from June to October of this year, since the government took power, a mere five-month period, the cost of fuel oil to heat homes, for instance, in Ottawa has risen 19 per cent, from 14 cents per litre to 17 cents per litre. The Ontario gate price for natural gas has risen 7 per cent, and the Tory government tells us that energy prices are going to take an even more drastic rise of $4 or more a barrel. But, Mr. Speaker, that is not the worst of it.
In the six months since the Conservatives took power the consumer loan interest rate has risen 18 per cent, from 13.5 per cent to 16.5 per cent. The rate of a first mortgage has skyrocketed by 30 per cent. It has risen from 10 per cent to 15 per cent.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TAX CREDIT IN RESPECT OF MORTGAGE INTEREST AND PROPERTY TAX
speechtext: Trying to clean up the mess.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TAX CREDIT IN RESPECT OF MORTGAGE INTEREST AND PROPERTY TAX
speechtext:
Indeed, it is fine to attempt to stimulate the housing market, but to claim to do so when the other policies that this government is following make it virtually impossible to buy and keep a home, is sheer lunacy.
November 28, 1979

The Conservatives are taking away with one hand what they have given with the other. This is not only fiscal irresponsibility, it is of the highest order of fiscal inconsistency, and this from a government which indicated that it would conduct a consistent, predictable fiscal policy supposedly to restore confidence in the economy. All they have done so far is to destroy that confidence.

Mr. Speaker, there is no doubt in my mind that this tax credit program is nothing more than a form of wasteful favouritism whose only result will be to deprive small businesses, research and development organizations as well as various industries of the investment they need, and in favour of whom? In favour of the housing industry which is in a relatively secure position in our country and which already benefits from very good programs. These tax credits are also a waste because they are part of a suspicious fiscal policy under the guise of a so-called home ownership assistance program. This is a tax cut and not legislation to improve the housing situation. 1 am concerned, therefore, when I realize that the money to finance this program will very likely come from the budget envelope marked for housing. Well, if the Progressive Conservative Party wants to spend this money on an item which is strictly a fiscal item, where will it find the necessary funds to meet the real needs of Canadians in the area of housing?
Mr. Speaker, this bill is a glaring injustice. Only a limited number of Canadians, between 16 per cent and 17 per cent, will get any substantial benefits from this bill. The other Canadians, including the have-nots, will be compelled to give their money to benefit a privileged few. Even the distribution of benefits among the various regions of Canada is unbalanced. Several provinces and communities will benefit much less than others. Try as we might to see it differently, it seems that the Progressive Conservatives, in the only program that they have suggested, supposedly to improve the housing situation in Canada, have succeeded in forgetting a number of people, including tenants, home owners who have finally paid off their mortgage after years of hardship, as well as all Canadians in the low income range. 1 shall come back to this aspect of the problem later on.

After the Prime Minister made his famous election promise, the critiques began rolling in. A group of MPs went to the U.S. to have a look at their mortgage deductibility scheme, and came back with horror stories. Then our economists took a close look at the Clark deductibility plans, and expressed concern and doubt. The C. D. Howe Institute, the Fraser Institute, the Canadian Institute for Economic Policy, University of Toronto economists, and others too numerous to mention, warned of the dangers of mortgage deductibility.
Mortgage Tax Credit
In February, 1979, the Liberal minister in charge of housing, the hon. member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), also warned us about mortgage deductibility and suggested alternatives of a shelter allowance and tax credit. Why was this suggestion not implemented then? Mr. Speaker, a responsible government could not see how we could get involved in almost $3 billion of new spending when so many other valuable programs called for so much expenditure and were a priority for us.
Having conducted the election campaign on a platform of mortgage interest deductibility, the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) modified the election promise to a mortgage and property tax credit scheme, on September 17, 1979. We on this side felt particularly gratified by the government's change of heart since more than a month earlier the hon. member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), myself, and the official opposition on urban perspectives, had made a recommendation. We had recommended that if, despite such opposition, the government was still intent on implementing its plan, it should modify it to become a tax credit scheme instead of a deductibility proposal. We only wish they had listened to us more closely and incorporated a shelter allowance concept so that more Canadians could benefit from the plan with the same amount of money.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, we must show some understanding and tolerance towards those on the government side. They made a commitment to keep what was a rather popular electoral promise for a time. The trouble is that by implementing a high interest rate policy, they have themselves changed this attractive plan into an extremely extravagant and unfair scheme. We also recognize that the average taxpayer must bear a tax burden that some consider disproportionate, but instead of promising him the moon, we prefer to allow him to make certain improvements to his home, with the help of the government if need be.
This bill is typical of the Progressive Conservative approach to social issues. They ignore Canadians facing real housing problems hoping that others will take care of them, while they try to help those with less pressing needs. This is the type of policy that we Liberals consider irresponsible and shortsighted. By promoting the disparities in the quality of housing, the government is only making the problem worse. The needs of low-income citizens multiply, often at the cost of social peace, which certainly does not improve the situation of middle-income citizens. The latter will benefit only from the shortterm advantages of a scheme which could have helped solve the real problems. Overpopulated urban centres, inadequate housing and the urban crime rate are some of the issues which have long concerned us. By turning their backs on the people who are faced with those problems, the Progressive Conserva-

November 28, 1979
Mortgage Tax Credit
tives are avoiding their responsibilities. This bill is just like their policy and attitude of hiding their heads in the sand.
Mr. Speaker, I want now to show this House and all Canadians the extent of the injustice of that proposal. The mortgage interest tax credit allows certain owners to claim a credit not exceeding 25 per cent of the first $5,000 paid in mortgage interest, to a maximum of $312.50 the first year gradually increasing to $1,250 in the fourth year. In 1979, some 4.5 million, or 48 per cent, of the 9,400,000 Canadian housing units were rented. So their occupants get absolutely nothing under this program. Furthermore, in 1977 some 2,570,000, or 27 per cent, owned mortgaged homes, and they too will not get anything at all under this program. Indeed, only 2,576,000 Canadians, or 33 per cent, of owners of mortgaged housing units were eligible for this program. In short, at least 67 per cent of Canadian households will not get a penny from this tax credit.

Citizens who do not pay income tax, a group which obviously includes the most underprivileged Canadians, get absolutely no benefit from this plan. They get no help at all in resolving their very acute housing needs. A family with two children would, under normal circumstances, have to earn more than $10,490 a year to get any mortgage interest tax credit. In order to receive the full credit in the first year of the program, such a family would have to earn at least $12,609, and for a full credit in the fourth year the family would have to earn the equivalent, in 1983, of $17,105. This means that many of the lowest income home owners will get nothing from this mortgage interest tax credit plan. Yet Statistics Canada has pointed out that in 1977 10 per cent of home owners holding a mortgage were in receipt of an income of less than $10,000, and that 25 per cent of them were receiving less than $15,000. People who pay less than $5,000 in mortgage interest will not be eligible for the full credit.
Not surprisingly, people with a higher income tend to take on larger mortgages to buy more expensive housing. Home owners with lower incomes often cannot afford to carry a mortgage on which they pay $5,000 in interest, that is, about $415 a month. Again we see that the people who need help most get least.

A great many Canadian tenants really need urgent help and are already feeling the effects of inflation and rising interest rates. This program will wipe out any hope of owning a home one day simply because they will not be able to afford it. From 1974 to 1979, the number of tenants whose rent accounts for more than 30 per cent of their income increased from 26 per cent to 28 per cent. Half of older citizens spend more than 25 per cent of their income on rent, as do 51 per cent of single-parent families. What will they get out of that mortgage rate deduction program? They can only expect to pay more taxes to subsidize those who will benefit under the program.


According to Statistics Canada, in 1977, 46 per cent of Canadian home owners did not carry a mortgage. Canadians who have worked hard for years to pay off their mortgages will suffer the same penalty of not benefiting from this scheme. Yet they, too, are under the pressures of rising inflation and energy and maintenance costs. Many of these people can hardly afford to keep the houses for which they have paid off their mortgages. The property tax credit will help them somewhat, and that is good, but they get no benefit from the larger mortgage credit.
What does that tell us about the Conservative government's apparent housing philosophy? It tells us we should not be thrifty or make great sacrifices to pay off our mortgages. We should carry our mortgage debt on to qualify for this program. Moreover, we should pay at least $5,000 in mortgage interest per year to get full benefit. This could actually be a disincentive to pay off a mortgage and could encourage more consumer debt.
The most serious problem in this legislation is that by its very nature it accentuates disparities across the country. The distribution of this tax credit in the different regions and provinces is highly unequal and disproportionate, largely because of the specific groups of Canadians at which it is aimed and because of the composition of types of accomodation in different regions.
Some regions of Canada will be indirectly subsidizing other regions. For example, in 1976 in Newfoundland, 80 per cent of householders were home owners, and only 19 per cent were renters. In British Columbia, 65 per cent were home owners, and 34 per cent were renters. In Ontario, 63 per cent were home owners, and 36 per cent were renters. However, in Quebec we find that only 50 per cent were home owners, and 49.6 per cent were renters.

speechtext: Then help them.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TAX CREDIT IN RESPECT OF MORTGAGE INTEREST AND PROPERTY TAX
speechtext:
It is apparent, therefore, that proportionately fewer Quebeckers will be eligible for this tax credit than Newfoundlanders, Ontarians, British Columbians or all other Canadians, but they will bear an equal burden of the cost of the credits. I think this is simply unfair.
Because the credit does not apply to those who have paid off their mortgages on the homes they own, as well as to renters, the benefits of the program are even more unevenly distributed. In Newfoundland, for example, 82 per cent of home owners do not have mortgages. In British Columbia the figure is 43 per cent. In Ontario it is 43 per cent, and in Quebec it is 41 per cent. We can therefore see that Newfoundlanders will be benefiting little while still sharing the cost.
The results are that the Atlantic region loses out because of the high percentage of people who own homes without mortgages, 70 per cent, and Quebec loses out because of the high percentage of renters, which is 49 per cent. Yet these are two of the areas which are in most need of housing assistance.
November 28, 1979

The mortgage interest tax credit program is so unevenly distributed that of the four provinces we have examined, Ontario, which has 36 per cent of Canada's population and 37 per cent of the nation's home owners, will receive 45 per cent of the benefits of the program. British Columbia, with 11 per cent of Canada's population and 12 per cent of the nation's home owners, will receive 16 per cent of the benefits. Newfoundland, with 2.4 per cent of Canada's population and 2.4 per cent of the country's home owners, will receive only 1.2 per cent of the benefits. And Quebec, with fully 27 per cent of Canada's population and 22 per cent of Canada's home owners, will receive only 19 per cent of the benefits.
We believe in the redistribution of wealth, but in redistribution to alleviate disparity, not to add to it. The unfair redistribution of this tax credit will create more regional disparity.

As I have already mentioned at least a couple of times, the home owner property tax credit, contrary to the mortgage interest tax credit, is more equitable. However, tenants are still being ignored. The scheme remains basically unfair to them because they will not get any direct benefit. Although more equitable, the home owner property tax credit could ultimately lead certain municipalities and provinces to increase their property tax rate and thus siphon off part of the benefits received by individuals. Should that ever be the case, some people could end up losing. Older people and owners with low incomes who do not pay federal taxes and are consequently not eligible for this credit could end up being even worse off.
The fact remains that this tax credit to home owners, amounting to as much as $62.50 in the first year of its implementation and $250 in the fourth, will be of significant help to several owners. But the universal aspect of the measure adds to its unfairness since a number of those who will benefit from it do not need assistance. When one compares that, Mr. Speaker, with the proposals of the Progressive Conservatives aimed at abolishing, reducing or revising family allowances, doing away with its universality, no longer reimbursing to mothers part of the expenses they have incurred in bringing up the Canadian generation of tomorrow, one wonders about the logic of those two measures!
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Crom-bie) says that people whose family income exceeds a certain level will get no help from the government to bring up their children. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Crosbie) says that they will get the mortgage interest credit only provided they belong to the category of those whose income is high enough.

Mr. Speaker, when we look through this bill we realize that in proposing a bill like this the Minister of Finance certainly has a lack of wisdom or lack of foresight, and a lack of imagination. He is hanging on at all costs to such a program. I cannot understand how somebody could vote for this bill as it is presented when we are expecting a budget, when the Minister of Finance tells us that Canadians will have to make
Mortgage Tax Credit
sacrifices, when inflation is going up, when the price of heating fuel is going to a record high and still will be higher, when the government talks about the reduction of social programs, and when it talks about unemployment going to 9.5 per cent in Quebec. 1 think this bill is an injustice.
I would say that we have made a very good effort in trying to convince the Conservative government that this bill should be changed, or perhaps postponed. Perhaps it should be re-written in order to be more just and to benefit many people. We have put up some 18 speakers. I think we have tried our best to convince the government of the unjust nature of the bill before us.
However, we do not want to be accused of filibustering such a bill. In conclusion, I think we cannot vote for such a bill, and we are ready if the government wants to vote now.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TAX CREDIT IN RESPECT OF MORTGAGE INTEREST AND PROPERTY TAX

speechtext:
It is an ideal Christmas gift that this government can bestow on a great number of members of the Canadian public.
One aspect of the program with which I am particularly pleased has to do with the property tax credit. Long before 1 came to this House I advocated such a scheme. 1 was the reeve of a small municipality for a great number of years, 26 years to be exact. I might say 1 was very, very young when 1 was first elected. I also served as vice-president of the Ontario Mayors and Reeves Association for a great number of years. Time and time again we passed resolutions addressed to the federal government of the day, requesting that municipal taxes on a home be deductible from income tax on the basis that it was an unfair arrangement in which the government was collecting a tax on tax. That was something that I had advocated in some of my earlier speeches in the House in 1972. 1 also brought that most emphatically to the attention of the former government. I see here the former minister responsible for housing. He is well aware of the fact that I had brought up this subject at that time. This is not an idea which was generated in the last six or eight months, or even last fall.
I can assure hon. members that this part of the tax is going to assist every home owner in Canada. According to what we

hear from over there, only the rich will benefit. I can assure members of the House that there are a great many senior citizens who live in their own homes and who probably find it difficult to get by, but who are still making enough money to pay taxes. They will certainly welcome this additional money they can spend.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE TAX CREDIT IN RESPECT OF MORTGAGE INTEREST AND PROPERTY TAX
speechtext: How about the renters?

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is now six o'clock, but 1 thought I should indicate to the House that there have been some discussions held with respect to the House business for the next few days. The first thing I should like to do-I guess the proper phrase would be-is to undesignate Friday, November 30, 1979, as an allotted day and indicate that it will be a day devoted to government business, for which I should like to thank the hon. opposition House leader. This would change the normal course of business for the balance of
Business of the House
the week. Because of certain indications I have received with respect to the debate on this bill, it would be our intention tomorrow to call the four references to select committees of the House of Commons, which stand in the names of various ministers, in the following order: rehabilitation, the review of the Foreign Investment Review Act, the review on the voluntary section and, finally, the cost overruns. That would be the order in which I would call them.
Also there have been discussions respecting the freedom of information legislation, so that that bill will be ready to go to committee. The understanding among my colleagues is that we could begin consideration of the freedom of information legislation tomorrow evening at eight o'clock, with the anticipation that the four references to select committees which I have mentioned, plus the second reading debate on the freedom of information legislation, could be completed by the close of business in the House on Monday evening. On the assumption and the understanding that in fact the debate is completed with respect to Bill C-20, it would be the hope of all of us that the vote, if there is to be one with respect to Bill C-20, would be in the early part of Tuesday afternoon. For that purpose, I inform the House that I will be calling Bill C-20 that day.
Further, with respect to the anticipation of the atmosphere of co-operation which 1 have found, and for which I am grateful, if any votes arise out of the four references-and I have some indication that there might be at least one-then that vote, or votes, would be held immediately afterwards. That is my anticipation of House business. In order to carry that forward, I hope we would be able to complete some things which are rather important to the government, and also move this bill into committee.
Also discussions have indicated that, as soon as the votes are completed, there is some anticipation that we would be moving into Committee of the Whole consideration of Bill C-20. I anticipate that will be generally agreeable to the House. It will be a way to advance the business of the House leading up to the adjournment, which I anticipate will take place on December 21. In any event, those are our plans at the moment.
Mr. Speaker, on the point of order relating to House business, it is true that there is a spirit of collaboration. The spirit was so great that we were even ready to vote tonight on Bill C-20.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I appreciate that.

We understand the debate is now adjourned, that it will continue next Tuesday, and that there might or might not be a vote on that day. I am not sure now. In any case, tomorrow and on Monday we will be dealing with the references suggested by the hon. government House leader. Also we will deal with the freedom of information bill tomorrow night at eight o'clock.
I want to make it very clear that it is true there is a spirit of co-operation, but I want it to be on the record that we told the
